Itemizing was the old way to reduce taxes. It's been nerfed and now small business is the new way. Figure out what category you spend the most in, and what business category deals in that category the most. For example, if you spend a ton of money on food, open up an 'online grocer', your food goes into inventory, and when it 'goes bad', you expense it on your taxes and 'dispose of it'. If you spend a ton of money repairing cars, open up an mechanics shop and expense your tools, repair parts, etc. If you spend the most money on your your house, things get trickier and involve trusts to be legit.

By the way, to make your business legit:

  • Make up some name (free)
  • Get a federal EIN for this name (free)
  • Open a bank account with this EIN, which will only be used for business purposes (~$50 - $500, but still your money)
  • (Optional step) Register your DBA or incorporate an LLC if it is cheap in your state. (~$50 - ~250)
  • (Recommended step) Buy a domain with your business name and wordpress it / pay someone to throw something together (~$50-100)

And you are now legally impenetrable. Legally penetrating your claims of business purpose requires proving you and the business are 'materially the same person', which is why you never mix between the business account and your personal account.

Also, the Fed uses a 3/5 test to determine whether your business is legit or a hobby. Hobby businesses have losses limited, which prevents you from deducting if on your 1040. The test is that you can't show losses for more than 3 of every 5 years (see page 7). Every 3 years, start a new one.
